characters.name: Aryan (The Narrator)
characters.who: A seasoned Forest Officer (Vanrakshak) with 5 years of experience in the dense tiger reserves.
characters.voice: First-person, steady, slightly weary but professional. He speaks as 'main' (I).

characters.name: Vikram
characters.who: A senior ranger who provides warnings about the local folklore and 'dead zones'.

bible.narration: First-person (main), past tense. The narrator is the forest officer experiencing the events.
bible.setting: A dense, remote tiger reserve in Central India during the monsoon season; specifically a 'no-go' zone where radio signals fail.
key_facts: The concept of 'Time Loops' or 'Echoes' in dense forests.
The psychological effect of isolation and auditory hallucinations.
Local belief in 'Aatma-Vani' (Soul Voices) that repeat past events.
motifs: The smell of damp earth and decaying leaves
bible.tone: Atmospheric, grounded, slow-burn horror. No jump-scares; the dread comes from the realization of a logical impossibility.
bible.ending: A chilling revelation about the timeline of the recording and the final moral to the audience.

sections.title: Ek Anokhi Duty
sections.purpose: Introductory sequence including mandatory greetings, context setting, and establishing the narrator's role.
beats: Mandatory greeting: 'Hello doston, mera naam hai Sudhansu aur aap dekh rahe hain Raat 3 Baje.'
Source disclosure: Mentioning it is based on a listener's experience of a forest officer.
Context setup: Describing the life of a vanrakshak and the isolation of the jungle.
Mandatory transition: 'Toh chaliye ab bina waqt zaya kiye aaj ki kahani ko sunte hain.'
The belief/twist hook: Mentioning how he once didn't believe in these things until his own experience.
Establishment of the setting: The year, the specific forest zone, and the upcoming patrol.

sections.title: Jungle Ki Khamoshi
sections.purpose: Establishing the atmosphere, the physical journey, and the first signs of 'wrongness'.
beats: Description of the patrol route into the deep forest (the 'Zone 4' area).
Sensory details: The humidity, the heavy silence, and the failure of radio communication.
Introduction of Vikram (senior ranger) and his warnings about 'echoes' in the valley.
The physical sensation of being watched by something not quite animal.
The first oddity: Hearing a sound that seems to repeat perfectly every 10 seconds.
The transition from day to dusk, where the forest feels physically heavier.

sections.title: Woh Ajeeb Awaz
sections.purpose: The core mystery: The discovery of the voice note and its disturbing nature.
beats: Stopping at a clearing to check equipment; finding a discarded, mud-caked walkie-talkie.
Hearing a burst of static followed by his own voice coming through the device.
The specific content: The narrator hears himself saying a sentence he only spoke that morning to a colleague.
The realization of the date/time on the recording—it matches today's date perfectly.
The discrepancy: In the recording, his voice sounds panicked and frantic, unlike his current calm state.
The realization that the 'voice' is coming from a location just a few meters away in the thicket.

sections.title: Gehrai Mein Dooba
sections.purpose: Escalation and the physical confrontation with the environment.
beats: The narration of his decision to investigate the source of the voice despite the warning.
The atmosphere changing: The forest sounds (insects, birds) suddenly cutting out completely.
The recording starts looping but begins to distort, layering multiple voices over one another.
Physical manifestation: Seeing shadows move in a way that contradicts the wind or movement of trees.
A moment of panic when he hears his own voice scream for help from 'inside' a tree trunk.
The frantic attempt to retreat as the sun sets and the 'echoes' become more frequent and louder.

sections.title: Sachayi Ka Khulasa
sections.purpose: The climax, the final twist, and the concluding moral.
beats: The discovery of a logbook or an old officer's ID at the source of the sound.
The realization: The recording isn't 'his' voice from today; it is his voice from 10 years ago (or another person who shared his name).
The twist: He realizes why the voice was so clear—it wasn't a recording, but a spatial fold.
The escape: Reaching the outpost and the lingering fear of 'hearing himself' in his sleep.
Final moral: 'Doston, zaroori nahi ki jis baat par tum yaqeen nahi karte, woh saari baatein jhooth ho.'
Closing line: 'Kabhi-kabhi doosron ki baaton par bhi yaqeen kar lena chahiye.'
